where: Worked example 1 and the figure (10 GHz, λg = 30 mm)
problem: At 10 GHz the free-space wavelength is 30 mm, so a guide wavelength of exactly 30 mm is only possible on an air-filled coaxial slotted line. In a rectangular waveguide λg is always greater than λ0 (about 40 mm in X-band guide at 10 GHz), so a student who assumes the slotted line is a waveguide will get a contradiction.
fix: Say which line is used: 'An air-filled coaxial slotted line at 10 GHz gives minima 15 mm apart, so λg = 30 mm, equal to the free-space wavelength.' Add that in a waveguide λg would be larger than λ0.

problem: 'A DC voltage appears at the cold junction' can be misread as if the cold junction alone generates the emf. The emf comes from the temperature difference between the two junctions.
fix: Write: 'RF power heats the hot junction while the cold junction is held at a fixed temperature; the thermocouple then produces a DC emf proportional to the temperature difference, and hence to the absorbed power, at its terminals.'

problem: 'the detector is square law, so work in voltage or take square roots of power readings' is muddled. A square-law detector output follows RF power; it is the meter calibration (volts or power) that decides how the readings must be treated.
fix: Write: 'The detector is square law, so its DC output follows RF power. Here the meter is calibrated in volts, so Vmax and Vmin are used directly; if the meter were calibrated in power, take square roots first.'

problem: Only the VSWR form of the square-root correction is given. A student with a power-calibrated meter also needs the corrected formula for |Γ|.
fix: Add: |Γ| = (√Mmax − √Mmin) / (√Mmax + √Mmin) when the meter reads power.
